title: Sell Mineral Rights in Tabiona, UT
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Tabiona, UT | Duchesne County
metaDescription: Own mineral rights near Tabiona, UT in the upper Uinta Basin? We buy Duchesne County ranching-family interests with a patient, no-pressure offer.
heroLead: Tabiona sits up the Duchesne River from the main Altamont-Bluebell action, a ranching community first and an oil town second, if at all.
intro: Most of the families we talk to around Tabiona have been on their land for generations, running cattle along the upper Duchesne River drainage rather than working in the oil field. Mineral ownership here tends to trace directly back to the original homestead patent, held by the same family that's still ranching the surface, which makes the title work simpler than in areas with a long history of speculative buying and selling.

That simplicity is worth something. When a mineral interest has stayed in one family's hands since the original patent, we can usually confirm the chain of title faster than in areas where the interest changed hands multiple times through unrelated transactions.

sections.heading: Upper basin position on the play
paragraphs: Tabiona sits toward the western and upper edge of the Uinta Basin, further from the dense Altamont-Bluebell core than Roosevelt or Myton, which generally means lighter well density and more modest per-acre values, though this varies by specific section and depth. We're upfront about that positioning rather than pricing a flank tract as though it were core acreage.

Ranching families here often value the surface use restrictions in any lease as much as the royalty terms, since active cattle operations don't want a well pad in the middle of a grazing allotment. That's a surface owner consideration, not a mineral owner one, but it's worth keeping in mind if you also hold the surface.

sections.heading: Homestead-era title, generations later
paragraphs: A patent issued to a great-grandparent under the Homestead Act or Desert Land Act typically passed mineral rights along with the surface unless a later deed specifically severed them. If your family has ranched the same ground since that original patent, there's a reasonable chance the mineral estate simply followed the surface through each generation's probate, intact.

We confirm this against the recorded chain at the Duchesne County courthouse in Roosevelt rather than assuming, since even long-held family land occasionally had a mineral severance somewhere in its history that heirs aren't aware of.

sections.heading: Selling without disrupting the ranch
paragraphs: A mineral rights sale doesn't touch surface ownership or grazing operations, and we structure the transaction so ranching families can sell the mineral interest, if they choose to, without any effect on how the land is used or run day to day. For some families that separation is exactly the point: liquidity from an asset that isn't part of the working ranch anyway.

faqs.question: Will selling my mineral rights affect our cattle operation on the same land?
faqs.answer: No. A mineral rights sale is entirely separate from surface ownership and grazing use. You keep full control of the ranch regardless of what happens with the mineral estate underneath it.

faqs.question: Is Tabiona-area acreage worth as much as land closer to Roosevelt?
faqs.answer: Generally it runs lower, since Tabiona sits toward the flank rather than the dense Altamont-Bluebell core, though the exact value depends on your specific section and depth.

faqs.question: How do we confirm the mineral rights actually followed our family's original patent?
faqs.answer: We research the recorded chain of title at the Duchesne County courthouse to confirm whether a severance ever occurred, rather than assuming the minerals simply followed the surface through each generation.
